title: Chapter 11.1 — Measures of Center and Variation

blocks.title: Calculating Center: Mean, Median, Mode
teacherCues: Display the eight wages: \$16.50, \$8.75, \$8.65, \$9.10, \$8.25, \$8.45, \$8.25, \$9.25. Ask: 'What’s a typical wage here? How many ways can we measure it?'
After students compute, ask: 'Which measure do you think is most fair – the \$9.65 average, the \$8.70 middle, or the \$8.25 most frequent?'

discoveryHook.scenario: A summer camp manager looks at the wages of eight student workers. The average is \$9.65, but only two people earn that much or more. The most common wage is \$8.25, yet that feels too low. Which number should they report? That’s the puzzle of mean, median, and mode.

explanation: A [[kw:measure of center]] summarizes a data set with a single typical value. The three most common are:
• Mean – the arithmetic average. Sum all values, then divide by the count. Symbol: $\bar{x}$.
• Median – the middle value when data are ordered. For an even number of values, average the two middle numbers.
• Mode – the value that appears most frequently. A data set can have one mode, several modes, or none.
Let’s apply these to the hourly wages: \$16.50, 8.75, 8.65, 9.10, 8.25, 8.45, 8.25, 9.25.
– Mean: $77.20 \div 8 = 9.65$. The average is \$9.65.
– Median: Sorted: $8.25, 8.25, 8.45, \mathbf{8.65, 8.75}, 9.10, 9.25, 16.50$. The middle pair averages to \$8.70.
– Mode: \$8.25 appears twice, more than any other value. The mode is \$8.25.
[[imp:Notice how the \$16.50 value pulls the mean upward but barely affects the median.]]

formulaCard.title: Mean, Median, Mode
formulaCard.formula: $$ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} \qquad \text{Median = middle value(s)} \qquad \text{Mode = most frequent value(s)} $$
notes: The mean uses every data point; sensitive to extreme values.
The median is robust – it only depends on order.
The mode is the only measure suitable for non‑numeric data.

examples.title: Example A – Find All Three Measures
steps: Order the numbers. The two middle values are 8.65 and 8.75. Median = (8.65+8.75)/2 = 8.70.
The only repeating value is 8.25 (twice). Mode = \$8.25.

examples.title: Example B – Choosing the Best Measure
examples.prompt: The three measures are \$9.65, \$8.70, \$8.25. Which one best represents a typical student’s wage?
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner: Why is the median often preferred when one value is much larger than the others?
steps: The \$16.50 wage is far above the rest – an outlier.
The mean is pulled up to \$9.65, which is higher than six of the eight wages.
The median (\$8.70) sits comfortably near the center of the ordered list and is a better reflection of a typical wage.

examples.title: Example C – Quick Practice
examples.prompt: Find the mean, median, and mode of: 12, 9, 17, 15, 10.
steps: Ordered: 9, 10, 12, 15, 17. Median = 12.
No value repeats → no mode.

confusionCorner.title: Always Sort Before Finding the Median!
confusionCorner.body: The median is not the 'middle' of the unsorted list – it's the middle of the ordered list. For an even number of data points, average the two central values.

questions.prompt: The mean of 2, 8, 9, 7, 6, 4 is the sum (36) divided by 6. The mean is ___.

hints: With nine values, the median is the 5th one.

questions.prompt: Does the data set 13, 30, 16, 19, 20, 22, 25, 31 have a mode? (yes/no)
hints: Check if any number appears more than once.

blocks.title: Outliers and Their Impact on the Mean
teacherCues: Circle the \$16.50 wage on the board. 'If we remove this one extreme value, how does the picture change?'
Recalculate mean and median without it. Show that the mean dropped by nearly a dollar, while the median barely moved.

discoveryHook.scenario: One student was hired as a web developer at \$16.50/hour, while the rest are game attendants around \$8–\$9. That single high wage inflates the 'average' wage. Removing it gives a far more honest look at what most workers earn.

explanation: An [[kw:outlier]] is a data value that is much larger or much smaller than the rest of the data.
• Effect on the mean: The mean is strongly influenced by outliers – it gets pulled toward them.
• Effect on the median: The median changes very little because it relies only on position, not magnitude.
• Effect on the mode: Usually unchanged unless the outlier itself repeats.
In the wage data, removing the \$16.50 outlier:
– New median: \$8.65 (down only \$0.05).
– Mode stays \$8.25.
[[imp:When a data set contains outliers, the median is often a more honest summary of the 'typical' value.]]

visuals.title: Wage Data With and Without the \$16.50 Outlier

formulaCard.title: Effect of Outliers
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Mean is sensitive to outliers; median is resistant.} $$
notes: Always inspect your data for outliers before choosing a summary statistic.
Report measures both with and without outliers when possible.

examples.title: Example A – Finding and Removing an Outlier
examples.prompt: Salaries (thousands): 32, 42, 41, 38, 38, 45, 72, 35. Identify the outlier and recompute the mean and median without it.
steps: Outlier: 72 is much higher than the rest.
With outlier: mean = 343/8 = 42.875, median = (38+41)/2 = 39.5.
Without outlier: mean = 271/7 ≈ 38.71, median = 38.
The mean dropped by ≈ 4.16; the median dropped by 1.5.

examples.title: Example B – Visualizing the Pull of an Outlier
examples.prompt: Why does an extreme value pull the mean so much more than the median?
examples.peerPrompt: Without looking at your notes, explain to a partner: Imagine balancing a ruler with coins placed at different positions. What happens if one coin is moved far to the right?
steps: The mean is like the balance point of the data – a far-away value acts like a heavy weight, tipping the balance toward itself.
The median is simply the middle position; changing one extreme value doesn't shift that position unless the order changes dramatically.

examples.title: Example C – Practice with Mass Data
examples.prompt: Masses of polar bears (kg): 455, 262, 471, 358, 364, 553, 62, 351. Identify the outlier and find the median without it.
steps: Outlier: 62 kg (much smaller).

confusionCorner.title: Not Every Outlier Should Be Removed!
confusionCorner.body: An outlier might be a genuine, important data point (like the CEO's salary). Only remove it if you have a clear reason, such as a measurement error. Otherwise, report the analysis both ways.

questions.prompt: An outlier is a value far from the others. Outliers affect the ___ much more than the median.
hints: It gets pulled toward extreme values.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Outliers affect the mean the most.

questions.prompt: In the salary data 32, 42, 41, 38, 38, 45, 72, 35 (thousands), what is the outlier? (type the number only)
hints: Look for the value that stands out.

questions.prompt: After removing the 62 kg outlier from the bear masses, what is the median mass?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Median without the outlier is 364 kg.

blocks.title: Measuring Spread: Range and Standard Deviation
teacherCues: Write two sets with the same mean: {0, 50, 100} and {49, 50, 51}. 'Both have mean 50, but how do they differ? How can we measure that difference?'
Introduce range = max − min. Then introduce standard deviation as a more refined measure of spread that uses every value.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two reality shows each have 12 contestants with an average age of 25. Show A's ages range from 19 to 31; Show B's from 19 to 48. The range tells part of the story, but the standard deviation reveals that a typical contestant on Show B is much further from the average age.

explanation: A [[kw:measure of variation]] describes how spread out the data are.
• Range = maximum value – minimum value. Simple, but only uses two numbers.
• Standard deviation (σ) measures the typical distance of a data value from the mean.
– Small σ → data are tightly clustered around the mean.
– Large σ → data are widely spread.

To compute σ: (1) Find the mean x̄. (2) Find each deviation x − x̄. (3) Square each deviation. (4) Find the mean of those squares (this is the [[kw:variance]]). (5) Take the square root of the variance.

visuals.title: Computing Standard Deviation for Show A Ages

formulaCard.title: Standard Deviation
notes: σ = 0 only when all values are identical.

examples.title: Example A – Compute Range and σ
examples.prompt: Show A ages: 20,29,19,22,25,27,27,29,30,20,21,31. Find the range and standard deviation.
steps: Range = 31 − 19 = 12 years.
Mean = 25. Sum of squared deviations = 212.
Interpretation: A typical contestant's age differs from the mean by about 4.2 years.

examples.title: Example B – Which Show Has More Variation?
examples.prompt: Show B ages: 19,20,21,22,22,24,25,25,27,27,32,48. Without calculating, which show has a larger range and likely a larger standard deviation?
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does the 48 inflate the standard deviation more than the range?
steps: Range: 48−19 = 29 (vs. Show A's 12).
The 48 is far from the mean, so its squared deviation is huge, greatly increasing the variance.
Thus Show B will have a larger standard deviation.

examples.title: Example C – Quick Practice
examples.prompt: Find the range and standard deviation of: 40, 35, 45, 55, 60. (Round σ to the nearest tenth.)
steps: Mean = 47. Deviations: −7,−12,−2,8,13. Squares: 49,144,4,64,169. Sum = 430. Variance = 86.

confusionCorner.title: Variance vs. Standard Deviation
confusionCorner.body: Variance is the mean of the squared deviations. Standard deviation is its square root, which brings the measure back to the original units (e.g., years, dollars). Always report standard deviation, not variance, when describing spread.

questions.prompt: The range of a data set is the difference between the greatest value and the ___ value.
hints: It's the smallest number in the set.

questions.prompt: In the standard deviation calculation, the mean of the squared deviations is called the ___.
If all values in a data set are the same, what is its standard deviation?
hints: There is no spread at all.

blocks.title: How Transformations Change the Statistics
teacherCues: Pose a scenario: 'Everyone gets a \$0.50 raise. What happens to the mean wage? To the spread?'
Then ask: 'What if everyone gets a 10% raise instead? Does the spread stay the same?'

discoveryHook.scenario: Adding a constant to every data value shifts the whole distribution without changing its shape. Multiplying stretches or compresses it. These simple rules let you update all your statistics instantly without touching the raw data.

explanation: A [[kw:data transformation]] applies the same operation to every value in a data set.
• Adding a constant k: All measures of center (mean, median, mode) increase by k. Measures of variation (range, σ) do not change.
• Multiplying by a constant k > 0: Every measure – center and spread – is multiplied by k.
Examples using the original wage statistics (mean \$9.65, median \$8.70, mode \$8.25, range \$8.25, σ = 2.61):
– After a \$0.50 raise: mean \$10.15, median \$9.20, mode \$8.75; range and σ unchanged.
– After a 10% raise (multiply by 1.1): mean \$10.62, median \$9.57, mode \$9.08; range \$9.08, σ = 2.87.

formulaCard.title: Data Transformations
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Add } k: \; \bar{x}_{\text{new}} = \bar{x} + k,\; \sigma_{\text{new}} = \sigma $$ $$ \text{Multiply by } k: \; \bar{x}_{\text{new}} = k\cdot\bar{x},\; \sigma_{\text{new}} = k\cdot\sigma $$
notes: Addition shifts the entire distribution; spread remains the same.
Multiplication stretches or shrinks the distribution proportionally.

examples.title: Example A – Adding a Constant
examples.prompt: Original wage measures: mean \$9.65, median \$8.70, mode \$8.25, range \$8.25, σ = 2.61. Each wage increases by \$0.50. Find the new measures.
steps: Range and σ are unchanged: \$8.25 and 2.61.

examples.title: Example B – Multiplying by a Constant
examples.prompt: Same original measures. Each wage increases by 10% (multiply by 1.1). Find the new measures.
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner: Why does multiplying change the standard deviation while adding does not?

examples.title: Example C – Practice with Addition
examples.prompt: A data set has mean 62, median 55, mode 49, range 46, σ = 15.5. Each value is increased by 14. Find the new measures.
steps: Range stays 46; σ stays 15.5.

confusionCorner.title: Range Also Scales with Multiplication
confusionCorner.body: Because range = max − min, and both max and min get multiplied by k, the range also multiplies by k. Don't forget it!

questions.prompt: If 5 is added to every value in a data set, the mean increases by ___.
hints: Adding a constant shifts all values equally.
The mean shifts by the same constant.

questions.prompt: If every value is multiplied by 3, what happens to the standard deviation? (Type: multiplied by 3, stays the same, or divided by 3)
hints: Multiplication scales both center and spread.
The spread stretches by the same factor.

questions.prompt: Original range is 12. Each value is multiplied by 0.5. What is the new range?

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Analyze Any Data Set
teacherCues: Summarize the workflow: Understand the context, Compute the five key measures, Choose the best summary, Conclude with interpretation.
Demonstrate on the wage data: Understand → note outlier; Compute → mean, median, mode, range, σ; Choose → median; Conclude → typical wage is about \$8.70, with a standard deviation of \$2.61.

discoveryHook.scenario: Faced with a new data set, the blueprint keeps you organized: check for outliers, calculate the measures, decide which center best tells the story, and interpret the spread. It's a repeatable process that turns raw numbers into meaningful insight.

explanation: 1. Understand: Identify the context and note any values that seem unusually high or low.
2. Compute: Find the five key numbers: mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation.
3. Choose: If outliers are present, the median is usually a more honest center. If the data are symmetric, the mean works well.
4. Conclude: Report the chosen center and the spread (range or standard deviation). Interpret what they mean in the real‑world situation.
This blueprint applies to test scores, sports stats, business metrics – any numerical data.

visuals.title: Blueprint Summary for the Wage Data

rows.2: \$16.50 is much higher → possible different job
Median (\$8.70) – not inflated by the high wage
A typical student earns about \$8.70; wages typically vary by \$2.61

formulaCard.title: Data Analysis Blueprint
notes: Report standard deviation alongside the mean when the data are symmetric.

examples.title: Example A – Full Blueprint on Wages
examples.prompt: Apply the blueprint to the eight summer wages.
steps: Understand: The \$16.50 wage is an outlier.
Compute: mean \$9.65, median \$8.70, mode \$8.25, range \$8.25, σ = 2.61.
Choose: Median (\$8.70) best reflects a typical wage.
Conclude: Most students earn around \$8.70, with wages varying by about \$2.61.

examples.title: Example B – Test Scores Without Outliers
examples.prompt: Test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95, 88. Analyze with the blueprint.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: Why is the mean a good choice here? How does the lack of outliers influence your decision?
steps: Understand: No extreme values; all scores between 68 and 95.
Compute: Mean = 83, median = 86.5, no mode. Range = 27, σ ≈ 10.3.
Choose: The mean (83) is representative because the scores are fairly symmetric.
Conclude: The average score is 83, with a typical deviation of about 10 points.

examples.title: Example C – Club Members' Ages
examples.prompt: Ages: 12,13,13,14,15,15,15,16,17,18,65. Use the blueprint to summarize.
steps: Understand: 65 is an outlier (perhaps an adult supervisor).
Compute: With outlier – mean ≈ 19.4, median = 15. Without – mean ≈ 14.8, median = 15.
Choose: Median (15) is unaffected by the 65.
Conclude: A typical club member is 15 years old.

confusionCorner.title: No Single Measure Tells the Whole Story
confusionCorner.body: Always pair a measure of center with a measure of spread. Saying 'the average is 83' is much more informative when you add 'and the standard deviation is about 10'.

questions.prompt: When a data set contains an outlier, the ___ is usually the best measure of center.
hints: It resists the pull of extreme values.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The median is usually best when outliers are present.

questions.prompt: For symmetric data without outliers, which measure of center uses all values and is most common? (mean, median, or mode)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The mean is the most common choice for symmetric data.

questions.prompt: If the standard deviation of a data set is 0, what must be true about the data? (one word)
hints: Every value is exactly the same.
